summary: VANTAGE shows which road segments of a corridor, if cut, leave communities without a route to a referral hospital, and for how long. It uses the OpenStreetMap road network, WorldPop population and NASA IMERG rain as context. Demonstrated on Ruta 32 (Costa Rica), the only corridor tested.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

VANTAGE answers a question that matters when a road closes: which segments of a corridor, if cut, leave communities without a route to a referral hospital, and for how long? For each critical segment (tramo crítico) it shows the extra travel time, the estimated population affected and the communities left without a route. Recent rain appears as context, labeled as a hypothesis.

A Python pipeline builds a road graph from OpenStreetMap for a configurable area. It removes one closure unit at a time (both carriageways, cut at every junction; 115 units on Ruta 32) and recomputes the fastest route from every community to the nearest referral hospital. WorldPop provides the population and NASA IMERG provides the rain. The pipeline writes JSON files and a static React + MapLibre web app reads them. A what-if simulation lets anyone close several segments at once and see the result instantly in the browser, with no backend and no account.

BENEFITS

It turns a road network into a clear picture of hospital access. Planners and emergency managers can see which segments matter most, so they can prioritize monitoring, maintenance and alternate routes before a closure happens. Everything is open and reproducible: each output can be traced to its inputs by SHA-256, and the site is static and free to host.

INTENDED IMPACT

To help decisions on road corridors where a closure can cut access to a hospital. The method is designed for any corridor with an OpenStreetMap road network: the area, reference hospitals, speeds and population raster are parameters, not code. Ruta 32 (Costa Rica) is our demonstration case and the only corridor we have tested.

TOOLS

Python (uv, pytest), TypeScript in strict mode, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, Bun, JSON Schemas for the shared data files, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. Data: NASA GPM IMERG, NASA/JPL NISAR GCOV, SMAP/NISAR SME2 soil moisture, OpenStreetMap, WorldPop CRI 2020, and the public OSRM router for a travel-time cross-check.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

We began with a bold idea: use NASA's new NISAR radar to spot landslide scars on a road corridor. We put it to the test with real data, and the evidence pushed us to a better question. Instead of guessing where a road might fail, VANTAGE measures what every possible cut would cost people in access to a hospital, for any segment, today.

That change turned the project into something more useful and more honest. Our radar, soil-moisture and rain tests became documented findings with their numbers, so other teams can build on them. The map now ranks 115 closure units by consequence, and a one-click simulation lets a user explore "what if this stretch closes?" in under 10 milliseconds. NASA rain data adds recent conditions as context for each segment. All of it runs from plain data files in a static website, which makes it easy to share, check and reuse on another corridor.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Reliability: we cross-checked travel times against a public router (median error 15.3% on 20 pairs), compared rankings under different speeds and hospital sets, and reviewed results by hand.

- The ranking depends on which hospitals count as the reference (three national hospitals in San José), so results are presented as access to those hospitals, not as general criticality.

- Travel times come from posted speed limits, so they are shown as orders of magnitude.

- Only Ruta 32 was tested.

- Wording: we use "critical segment", "signal" and "hypothesis". We never claim a confirmed closure or a cause.
